```text
   Anyone with any level of poker experience knows that the game has a
number of variables baked into it that make it psychologically challenging.
First, you have to take risks under conditions of uncertainty. Second, you
must manage the consequences of taking those risks. Third, there is no
way you will ever come close to winning all the hands or sessions you
play. Your goal is to maximize your expectation, but that expectation is
going to be a long way from 100%. Above all else, you still have to deal
with stresses and strains of life both at the table and away from it.
   Because humans are hardwired to prefer certainty over uncertainty,
taking financial risks in an ambiguous situation with imperfect information
and potentially large consequences takes a toll. A whole host of mental
processes kick in that can influence decision making and behavior in ways
that lead to plays that are sub-optimal. Factors that can impact perform-
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance


   ♠ emotions
   ♠ mood
   ♠ thoughts, beliefs and perceptions
   ♠ ability to sustain attention and focus
   ♠ hormone and neurochemical levels
   ♠ habits and patterns of behavior
   ♠ recent performance
   ♠ environment.

   On top of all this, the games have got tougher and competition has in-
creased dramatically. Add in information overload and stressors that have
nothing to do with poker (like problems with family members or jobs) and
you can see that mastering the mental game is a tall order. This chapter is
going to offer you information that, if acted upon, can assist you in devel-
oping your mental and emotional skills as well as enhance your decision
making.

Your Mindfulness Baseline
Before we get into some of the techniques you can use to help win your
mental battles, it would be helpful to assess your current level of mindful-
ness. Mindfulness is the most important aspect of developing a strong
mindset, and the cornerstone of the mindset strategies outlined below.
Dr. Kirk Brown developed the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS)
to act as an indicator of mindfulness (Figure 1). People who score high on
this scale are more aware of their thoughts and feelings, have more cog-
nitive control and have more control over their behavioral responses than
those who score low on the scale.
```

```text
                                           Transform Your Mental Game

formation given in this chapter for a few weeks, you can reassess yourself

Developing Psychological
Flexibility: Mindfulness Training
To gain control over your mind you need to develop a set of psychological
skills that are collectively known as psychological flexibility. Generally
speaking, if you are high in psychological flexibility, you’ll be able to deal
with negative experiences effectively. Studies have shown that people
with higher levels of psychological flexibility experience fewer psychologi-
cal problems, more positive emotions, greater career success, better
relationships, and an overall higher quality of life. They cope better with
setbacks, and recover faster from all kinds of losses and difficulties.
    One study in particular was conducted with high level international
chess players who were taught mindfulness approaches. The participants
showed significant reductions in interference caused by unpleasant
thoughts, feelings, emotions, and impulses during competitions. They also
showed reductions in the use of counterproductive reactions to negative
experiences compared to their previous reactions. They were still reaping
the benefits of the intervention in improved chess performance seven
months after their mindfulness training protocol ended. A control group
of matched chess players did not get training in mindfulness, and at their
seven month follow-up none had improved their performance. There
have been similar studies undertaken with athletes, law enforcement offi-
cers, and members of the military that have all shown similar results. On
the whole, learning approaches that increase psychological flexibility tend
to provide substantial benefits.
    Psychological inflexibility, on the other hand, is the tendency to ignore,
deny, or avoid things that are hard for us. It’s linked to coping poorly, long
recovery times, and high rates of addiction. No one likes failure, but we all
have negative experiences at the table. I’m going to offer some strategies
here, which can be experimented with to get rid of or manage emotions.
You need to be able to have a good session even when they pop up.
```

## PDF page 167

```text
Peak Poker Performance

   There are two key components to psychological flexibility: increased
awareness of the things that cause you trouble and a willingness to try
new strategies. The best way to develop psychological flexibility is by be-
ing fully aware by practicing mindfulness.
   Elliot Roe and I had Tommy Angelo on a recent podcast of The Mindset
Advantage, and when I asked about the easiest way for poker players to
become more mindful, he offered these instructions:

      The simplest and most effective thing is sitting up straight
      while you’re playing, whether it’s online or live. That means any
      awareness of your posture, whatsoever, is a moment of mind-
      fulness. And so if you find yourself slouching and then you sit
      up straight, even if it’s for two seconds, in my opinion, that’s a
      moment of full awareness. That’s exactly as aware as any monk
      has ever been. And then, we get lax, we slack off, and our body
      becomes mindless, and we don’t know where our arms and
      hands are. And then all of a sudden we remember. “Oh, I’m go-
      ing to consciously put my feet flat on the floor. I’m going to
      consciously raise my chest up.” That to me is the most effec-
      tive act that any poker player could ever do in any game.

    Mindfulness is an ancient concept found in a wide range of spiritual and
religious traditions, but it doesn’t have to be religious. You can bring mind-
fulness to any activity including poker, as Angelo so clearly shows. Mindful-
ness simply means paying attention with flexibility, openness, and curiosity.
    It’s an awareness process, not a thinking process. It involves bringing
awareness or paying attention to your experience in this moment, as op-
posed to getting caught up in your thoughts. It involves an attitude of
openness and curiosity. Even if your experience is difficult and painful, you
can be open to and curious about it instead of fighting it. Mindfulness also
involves flexibility of attention. It teaches you the ability consciously to di-
rect, broaden, or focus your attention on different aspects of your experi-
ence.


166
```

```text
                                           Transform Your Mental Game

    We can use mindfulness to connect with ourselves and appreciate the
fullness of each moment; to improve our self-knowledge in order to learn
more about how we feel, think, and react; and to consciously influence
our own behavior. Research shows that being mindful, or present, is a
profound way to enhance psychological resilience and increase life satis-
faction. It allows us to live and play with much more consciousness and
awareness, and is strongly correlated with peak performance.
    The longer you practice being mindful, the more you’ll realize that
negative thoughts and experiences are simply a natural part of life. Even
when we are running bad or feeling angry, we don’t have to let those ex-
periences and sensations ruin our session. You can pay close attention to
your negative thoughts, feelings, and experiences. You don’t have to try
to deny, avoid, or suppress them. If we develop our capacity for mindful-
ness, we can embrace calm acceptance. Even though every human has
this capacity, most of us rarely cultivate it. The result is that we are dis-
tracted, preoccupied with thoughts about the past and future, inefficient,
and stressed out. We so often operate on “automatic pilot” that we do
not actualize our goals and values.
    Many people think that the only way to cultivate mindfulness is to
meditate, and while meditation is a fine practice, you can actually bring
mindfulness to any endeavor. Angelo also spoke on our show about how
he incorporates mindfulness more fully into his playing sessions:

         When I’m playing poker, I have gotten to where I’m ex-
      tremely mindful. I would say, mindful is a hard word to define,
      but I would say I am aware of my breathing or my posture
      about 75% of the time, which is a huge, huge number. I would
      say in the course of regular life, it’s closer to 5% of the time.
      What I’ve done with poker for 10 years now, I’ve actually
      made it a meditation practice. That’s one of the reasons I go
      there is with the objective of being mindful.
         One of my tools I’ve been using the last three years is my
      object of the game now when I play... to observe every bet-
      ting action on every street.
```
